cue: Everything is one shade, with a sharp band across the middle and a very wide field.

cpd.note: a squid's measured value, used by the app for the whole picture

fov.note: the field measured in oval squid from three weeks old, which holds between 323 and 329 degrees; the squeeze toward this width is the app's

M.note: one visual pigment; the mapping to the screen is the app's

CEPHALOPOD_ONE.note: one pigment peaking near 480 nanometres, so the picture has a single shade

frac.note: how tall the sharp band is on the screen; the app's choice

cpd.note: an octopus's measured acuity, given to the sharp band by the app; the rest of the picture takes a squid's

field.name: squeeze
field.note: the whole field squeezed into the picture

rows: An octopus resolves about 12 cycles per degree and a squid about 6.6, against a person's 30. Some small octopus species fall between 3 and 7, a cuttlefish is put near 8, and a newly hatched oval squid manages only 0.63. The picture is blurred to a middling value for adults.

Almost all of these animals have a single visual pigment, with its peak between 470 and 500 nanometres, near 480 in octopus. With one pigment they cannot tell hues apart, and tests on octopus and on cuttlefish agree. The picture keeps one shade and only the brightness changes.

Oval squid from three weeks old see about 323 degrees around themselves. One eye of a cuttlefish covers 253 degrees, and the two eyes of a cuttlefish overlap by 86 degrees in front. Octopuses have no significant overlap. The camera holds a slice of this wide field.

The receptors of an octopus are packed most densely in a horizontal stripe across the middle of the retina, about 55,000 per square millimetre against 18,000 to 22,000 at the edge. Cuttlefish and squid also have a streak or a patch of crowding. A sharp band runs across the picture.

An octopus pupil is round in the dark and shrinks to a horizontal slit in bright light, down to about a tenth of its dark area. A cuttlefish can shrink its pupil to 3 percent of the widest opening. The picture uses the slit.

A squid stops seeing flicker near 51 a second in dim light and a cuttlefish near 30. An octopus reaches 72 in bright light and only 20 when the light is far dimmer. A person stops near 60, so these flicker limits are close to yours or lower and the picture keeps your pace.

Octopuses pick out differences in the direction of polarised light that a person cannot see at all. Their eyes have two sensitive planes, one horizontal and one vertical, and the typical octopus threshold is very fine. A phone camera records none of this, so the picture leaves it out.

The squid value of 6.56 for the whole picture, the width of the squeezed field, the height of the sharp band, the sharpness given to that band and the single-shade mapping are the app's own settings, placed inside what the records describe.
